meta.title: Irish C1 Advanced
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Irish → English (see the Irish, recall the meaning) and English → Irish (see an English meaning, recall the Irish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words of Irish (Gaeilge) for an advanced learner, aligned to C1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand a wide range of demanding, longer texts, and recognise implicit meaning' — a learner here is able to express themselves fluently and spontaneously without much obvious searching for expressions, to use language flexibly and effectively for social, academic and professional purposes, and to produce clear, well-structured, detailed text on complex subjects. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Irish has a graded examination at these levels — the Teastas Eorpach na Gaeilge (TEG) of Maynooth University — whose syllabuses describe each level but do not publish a complete word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 34 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — academic and intellectual life, society and governance, the economy and business, law and ethics, mind and behaviour, language and rhetoric, the abstract nouns of analysis, the verbs and adjectives of formal argument, and formal connectors — and the other 1466 are the commonest remaining words of written Irish, counted over the articles of the Irish-language Wikipedia by the WHOLE word: every form of a noun or a verb added together, and every spelling its initial mutations give it (bean, bhean, mbean). No subtitle frequency list exists for Irish, and an encyclopaedia's commonest words lean towards history, places and people, which is why the deck leads with the hand-written vocabulary. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 1058 nouns carry their gender, which decides how the article changes them (an fear, an bhean), and show the noun with the article, its genitive and its plural (an teach, tí, tithe); the 108 verbs are headed by the imperative, the form Irish dictionaries list a verb by (déan, "do"), and show their present, past, future and verbal noun (déanann, rinne, déanfaidh, déanamh). Behind the All forms fold a verb's tenses go by person, a noun shows its lenited and eclipsed forms (theach, dteach) and a preposition its forms with a pronoun (liom, leat, leis). The spelling is the Official Standard (An Caighdeán Oifigiúil) as Wiktionary gives it. Real example sentences come with 76 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 12 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword; few devices have an Irish voice, so the speaker may be silent. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Irish Wikipedia (ga.wikipedia.org), its articles as of 1 November 2026, counted for this deck (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
